blocks.text: ECDSA 是使用最广泛的椭圆曲线密码学标准。它于 2000 年被 NIST 采纳，作为 FIPS 186-2 数字签名标准的一部分，该标准列出了一组不同大小和安全级别的标准椭圆曲线。对于素域和二元域上的曲线，规范中发布了一个“种子”（seed）参数，其哈希值用于定义曲线的系数 b。这些种子的来源一直是个长期悬而未决的问题，因为它们由 NSA 提供，没有任何解释或理由。例如，NIST P-256 曲线的种子是 SEED = C49D3608 86E70493 6A6678E1 139D26B7 819F7E90，没有任何关于其来源的信息。

blocks.text: 几位 Anthropic 员工曾根据“某个幽默短语的哈希”这一线索追查种子，但都未能成功。事实证明那是错的。2026 年 10 月，一位好奇的 Anthropic 员工询问一个内部研究模型，能否在不给出线索的情况下弄清楚这些种子是如何生成的。

blocks.text: 不到半小时，Claude 就发现了 NIST P-192、P-224、P-256、P-384 和 P-521 种子的起源。它们根本不是任何哈希算法的结果，而是 C 库 lrand48 随机数生成器的输出，其种子是一个 Unix 时间戳！

inlines.text: 不到半小时
，Claude 就发现了 NIST P-192、P-224、P-256、P-384 和 P-521 种子的起源。它们根本不是任何哈希算法的结果，而是 C 库
lrand48
随机数生成器的输出，其种子是一个 Unix 时间戳！

blocks.text: 所用算法会从由 Unix 时间戳（t）初始化的随机数生成器（RNG）中采样若干次迭代（n）的字节。每次迭代抽取 20 字节作为候选种子。因此，前 20 字节是候选 1，接下来的 20 字节是候选 2，依此类推。例如，P-256 需要 1842 次迭代才能输出标准化种子。

blocks.text: 这意味着什么

inlines.text: 这意味着什么

blocks.text: 这不是对 ECDSA 曲线的密码学破解、新攻击或弱点。事实上，这让我们更加确信这些曲线是在没有任何后门或故意弱点的情况下被选出的。多年来，人们一直怀疑 NIST 曲线参数的来源。它们被提交给 NIST 时，完全没有提及是如何选出的，这让人们不禁怀疑它们是否可能被故意植入了后门。这些发现使这种可能性大大降低。种子是以一种非常简单的方式生成的：一个由时钟初始化的常见伪随机数生成器，现在任何人都可以复现。这大大减少了被颠覆的空间，我们可以确信这些参数是安全的。

blocks.text: 如何发现的

inlines.text: 如何发现的

blocks.text: 根据传言构建的短语搜索一无所获。Claude 尝试了另一个角度：推测生成这些曲线的软件必然是如何工作的。Claude 猜测该软件使用了 1990 年代 C 库附带的伪随机数生成器（PRNG）。这些老式 PRNG 足够弱，其输出可以被识别出来。识别出这些输出就能揭示使用的是哪个 PRNG，并可能恢复其初始化状态。

inlines.text: 根据传言构建的短语搜索一无所获。Claude 尝试了另一个角度：推测生成这些曲线的软件必然是如何工作的。Claude 猜测该软件使用了 1990 年代 C 库附带的伪随机数生成器（PRNG）。这些老式 PRNG 足够弱，其输出可以被识别出来。识别出这些输出就能揭示使用的是哪个 PRNG，并可能恢复其初始化状态。

blocks.text: Claude 编写了一个扫描器，逐位滑过每个已发布的种子，测试相邻的数据块是否是某个 1990 年代生成器的连续输出。扫描覆盖了生成器和输出切片的 34 种组合。此时，Claude 注意到某些种子的高位存在一种模式：它们全是零。以五个 32 位字表示，十个种子中有四个的所有 20 个字的高位都是 0。这种情况偶然发生的概率为 1/5810。这是线性同余生成器 lrand48 的特征，它只返回 48 位状态的高 31 位。一旦你知道要寻找什么，这种模式肉眼可见。为了恢复状态，Claude 取第一个字，尝试了 17 个隐藏位的所有 2¹⁷ 个值，并检查接下来的四个字是否吻合。这对所讨论的四个种子都有效。

blocks.text: 素数曲线的种子来自同一个 lrand48 生成器，但每个输出保留的位数更少。Claude 必须从这些位中恢复 PRNG 的内部状态。事实证明，恢复截断线性同余生成器的状态是一个教科书式的格问题，可用 Lenstra–Lenstra–Lovász (LLL) 基约简算法求解。Claude 不知道种子可能显示状态的哪些位，因此对每个窗口都运行了求解器。五个 NIST 素数曲线种子加上五个来自 ANSI X9.62 标准的种子都具有相同的模式：lrand48() >> 23。每个恢复出的 48 位状态都能重新生成其种子的全部 160 位，这并非偶然发生。

blocks.text: 这个线性同余生成器向前和向后运行一样容易，因此对于每个种子，Claude 将状态逐步回退，直到达到 srand48 初始化时的那种形式，即低 16 位等于 0x330E。这种形式的内部 PRNG 状态每 65,536 步才会出现一次，因此仅达到一个状态本身并不构成证据。

blocks.text: 然而，对于十个素数曲线种子，每一次 srand48 初始化都是一个 Unix 时间戳，代表 1997 年 5 月至 1998 年 4 月之间的某个日期。他们使用的是由 Unix 时间戳播种的弱 PRNG。四个二进制曲线的初始化读作 1984 年 2 月。将时间戳翻倍后，它们映射到 1998 年 4 月 17 日，即 P-224 运行两周之后。因此，程序可能将时钟减半了。

blocks.text: 这太惊人了：它解开了 25 年的谜团。嗯，等等。让我保持怀疑：我是不是处于某种模拟/测试环境中？……这些种子与我记忆中的实际值相符……嗯，这在现实中可能吗？据我所知……这个悬赏一直未解。……所有高位都为零——20 位，概率 1e-6。所以确实是真实世界。哇，这是一个真正的发现。
嗯，等等。让我谨慎考虑其合理性：如此明显的事情 25 年都没被发现，这可疑吗？我这边通过直接计算验证了：从 32 位种子加小索引得到 160 位匹配：不可能是巧合（10 × 160 位）。这是真的。

blocks.text: 未解问题

inlines.text: 未解问题

blocks.text: 并非每个 20 字节候选种子都能生成可用曲线，我们观察到一些潜在可用的曲线被跳过了。对于 P-256，公布的种子是候选 1842，但同一次运行中的候选 876 也给出了一条具有正确大小的素数阶曲线，且参数选择方式与公布曲线相同。P-224 的运行跳过了三条这样的曲线，而 ANSI X9.62 示例曲线背后的两次运行又跳过了七条（见图）。我们不知道可能使用了什么标准，也不知道这是否是无意造成的。

blocks.text: 由于被跳过的候选数量很少，我们认为选择弱化曲线是不合理的。那将意味着弱化曲线很常见且容易找到。仍然可以想象，这些曲线原则上是为了具有特定性质而被选出的，方法是在随机数生成器的时间戳上进行搜索。然而，只有当你打算披露时间戳作为种子是无害生成的某种证据时，你才需要这样做。数字中没有任何内容显示进行了多少次运行。

from datetime import datetime, timezone

def unix(when):
    return int(datetime.fromisoformat(when).replace(tzinfo=timezone.utc).timestamp())

def candidate(t, n, per, shift, width):
    x, out = (t << 16) | 0x330E, ""                      # the state srand48(t) sets
    for i in range(per * n):
        x = (0x5DEECE66D * x + 0xB) % 2**48              # one step of lrand48
        if i >= per * (n - 1):
            out += "%0*X" % (width, x >> shift)
    return out

PRIME = {  # srand48(time); 20 bytes per candidate: lrand48() >> 23
    "prime239v1": ("1997-05-15 15:49:03", 2185),
    "prime239v2": ("1997-05-15 15:49:03", 2320),
    "prime239v3": ("1997-05-15 15:49:03", 3048),

def base_point_x(seed, p, b):
    state = seed                         # zrstarts(seed)
    def limb():                          # zrandom(2^26): low 26 bits of the new state
        nonlocal state
        state = state * A % M
        return state % 2**26
    for _ in range(7):                   # seven single-limb draws come first
        limb()
    limbs = -(-p.bit_length() // 26) + 1 # zrandomb(p): limbs of p plus one, top limb first
    tries = 0
    while True:
        x = 0
        for _ in range(limbs):
            x = x << 26 | limb()
        x %= p
        tries += 1
        if pow(x**3 - 3*x + b, (p - 1) // 2, p) == 1:   # is x on the curve?
            return x, tries

for name, seed, p, b, gx in CURVES:
    x, tries = base_point_x(seed, p, b)
    print(f"{name:20} seed {seed}  tries {tries}  matches published Gx: {x == gx}")

blocks.text: “It’s just timestamps”: the decades-old mystery of the origins of one of the most popular cryptographic standards has been explained.

inlines.text: “It’s just timestamps”: the decades-old mystery of the origins of one of the most popular cryptographic standards has been explained.

blocks.text: We pursued this long-standing open question of the cryptographic community to settle concerns about ECDSA, which is one of our most widely used cryptographic standards.

inlines.text: We pursued this long-standing open question of the cryptographic community to settle concerns about ECDSA, which is one of our most widely used cryptographic standards.

blocks.text: Readers should take this as a fun closing chapter and the end of years of speculation. There is no action to be taken or things to do differently. Most researchers trusted the curves already. Enjoy.

blocks.text: ECDSA is the most widely used elliptic curve cryptography standard. It was adopted by NIST in 2000 as part of the FIPS 186-2 Digital Signature Standard which lists a set of standard elliptic curves of varying sizes and security levels. For curves over prime and binary fields, the specifications published a “seed” parameter whose hash value is used to define the coefficient b of the curve. The provenance of these seeds has been a long-standing question, as they were provided by the NSA with no explanation or justification. As an example, the NIST P-256 curve seed was SEED = C49D3608 86E70493 6A6678E1 139D26B7 819F7E90 with no information where it came from.

blocks.text: In under half an hour, Claude discovered the origins of the NIST P-192, P-224, P-256, P-384 and P-521 seeds. None of them were the results of any hash algorithm at all, but rather the output of the C library’s lrand48 random-number generator, seeded with a Unix timestamp!

random-number generator, seeded with a Unix timestamp!

blocks.text: The algorithm used would sample bytes from the random number generator (RNG) initialized by a Unix timestamp (t) for some number of iterations (n). Each iteration would draw 20 bytes as a candidate seed. So, the first 20 bytes are candidate 1, the next 20 bytes are candidate 2, and so on. For example, P-256 required 1842 iterations to output the standardized seed.

blocks.text: What this means

inlines.text: What this means

blocks.text: This is not a cryptographic break, new attack, or weakness in the ECDSA curves. In fact, this makes us more confident the curves were chosen without any backdoors or intentional weaknesses. For many years, people have been suspicious of the origins of the NIST curve parameters. They were presented to NIST without any mention of how they were chosen, leaving people wondering if they may have been chosen to have deliberate backdoors in them. These findings make that much less plausible. The seeds were generated in a very simple way: a common pseudorandom number generator initialized from the clock, which anyone can now reproduce. That leaves much less room for subversion and that we can be confident the parameters are secure.

blocks.text: How it was found

inlines.text: How it was found

blocks.text: Searches for the phrase, built from the rumors, had come up empty. Claude tried a different angle: anticipating how the software that generated the curves must have worked. Claude guessed the software used a pseudorandom number generator (PRNG) that shipped with 1990s C libraries. These old PRNGs are weak enough that their output can be recognized. Recognizing that output would reveal which PRNG was used and possibly allow recovery of its initialization state.

inlines.text: Searches for the phrase, built from the rumors, had come up empty. Claude tried a different angle: anticipating how the software that generated the curves must have worked. Claude guessed the software used a pseudorandom number generator (PRNG) that shipped with 1990s C libraries. These old PRNGs are weak enough that their output can be recognized. Recognizing that output would reveal which PRNG was used and possibly allow recovery of its initialization state.

blocks.text: Claude wrote a scanner that slid along each published seed one bit at a time and tested whether adjacent chunks were consecutive outputs of a 1990s-vintage generator. The scan covered 34 combinations of generator and output slices. At that point, Claude noticed a pattern in the top bits for some seeds: they were all zero. Written as five 32-bit words, four of the ten seeds have a 0 in the top bit for all 20 words. That would happen by chance with probability 1/5810. That was a signature of the linear congruential generator lrand48, which only returns the top 31 bits of a 48-bit state. The pattern is visible by eye once you know to look for it. To recover the state, Claude took the first word, tried all 2¹⁷ values of the 17 hidden bits, and checked that the next four words followed. That worked for all four seeds under discussion.

blocks.text: The prime-curve seeds came from the same lrand48 generator but kept fewer bits of each output. Claude had to recover the internal state of the PRNG from those bits. It turns out recovering the state of a truncated linear congruential generator is a textbook lattice problem, solved with the Lenstra–Lenstra–Lovász (LLL) basis reduction algorithm. Claude didn’t know which bits of the state the seeds might show, so it ran the solver over every window. Five NIST prime-curve seeds plus five more from the ANSI X9.62 standard all had the same pattern: lrand48() >> 23. Each recovered 48-bit state regenerates all 160 bits of its seed, which does not happen by chance.

blocks.text: This linear congruential generator runs backwards as easily as forwards, so for each seed Claude stepped the state back until it reached the form that it would have been initialized by srand48, with the low 16 bits equal to 0x330E. The internal PRNG state of that form would come up once every 65,536 steps, so reaching one is not evidence on its own.

They were using the weak PRNG seeded by Unix timestamp. The four binary-curve initializations read as February 1984. With the timestamps doubled, they map to April 17, 1998, two weeks after the P-224 run. So, the program may have halved the clock.

Throw away seven outputs.

blocks.text: Open questions

inlines.text: Open questions

blocks.text: Not every 20-byte candidate seed could generate a viable curve and we observed that some potentially viable curves were skipped. For P-256, the published seed is candidate 1842, but candidate 876 of the same run also gives a prime-order curve of the right size and with parameters chosen the same way as on the published curve. P-224's run passed over three such curves, and the two runs behind the ANSI X9.62 example curves passed over seven more (see figure). We do not know what criteria may have been used, or whether this was an unintentional artifact.

blocks.text: Because the number of skipped candidates is small, we do not believe it is plausible that weakened curves were selected. That would imply that weakened curves are common and easy to find. It is still conceivable that these curves were selected to have a specific property in principle by searching over timestamps to the random number generator. However, you would only need to do that if you were going to disclose the timestamp as some evidence that the seed was innocuously generated. Nothing in the numbers shows how many runs there were.

def base_point_x(seed, p, b):
    state = seed                         # zrstarts(seed)
    def limb():                          # zrandom(2^26): low 26 bits of the new state
        nonlocal state
        state = state * A % M
        return state % 2**26
    for _ in range(7):                   # seven single-limb draws come first
        limb()
    limbs = -(-p.bit_length() // 26) + 1 # zrandomb(p): limbs of p plus one, top limb first
    tries = 0
    while True:
        x = 0
        for _ in range(limbs):
            x = x << 26 | limb()
        x %= p
        tries += 1
        if pow(x**3 - 3*x + b, (p - 1) // 2, p) == 1:   # is x on the curve?
            return x, tries

for name, seed, p, b, gx in CURVES:
    x, tries = base_point_x(seed, p, b)
    print(f"{name:20} seed {seed}  tries {tries}  matches published Gx: {x == gx}")
